title: The Exiled General Who Wrote for All Time
author: Thucydides
wiifm: Why do powerful, sophisticated societies talk themselves into ruinous decisions? Thucydides watched his own city, Athens, do exactly that, and wrote it down with a coldness that still startles. He shows fear driving rivals to war, a plague breaking a society's morals, crowds voting for massacre and then for an overreaching adventure that destroyed them. We follow a wealthy Athenian who caught the plague, lost a battle, was exiled for twenty years, and used the time to write what he called a possession for all time.

ch.h: A rich man's son in a golden age
b: Thucydides was born in Athens around 460 BC, the son of a man named Olorus. That name is a clue. It was Thracian, and the family seems to have been related to the old Athenian statesman Cimon and to have owned the rights to gold mines in Thrace, on the northern coast of the Aegean. So this was a wealthy, well connected young man.

He grew up in the most extraordinary moment of Athenian history. The Persians had been beaten back a generation earlier. Athens now led a league of island and coastal cities that had begun as a voluntary alliance and was hardening into an empire, collecting tribute from its allies and using it, among other things, to build the Parthenon. The city's leading politician was Pericles, a brilliant speaker who dominated the democratic assembly for thirty years.

Thucydides says almost nothing about his own youth. He tells us his name, his father's name, and that he was an Athenian. Everything else we must piece together from a handful of remarks in his history. But we know he would have watched the democracy at work on the Pnyx hill, thousands of citizens voting on war and peace, and that what he saw there became the subject of his life.

He was also growing up in the age of the first great historian, Herodotus, who wrote about the Persian Wars with gods, oracles, marvels and wonderful digressions. Thucydides would set himself firmly against that style. He wanted no gods intervening and no fabulous tales. He wanted to explain events through human decisions, human nature and the pressures of power.
ch.cap: Young Thucydides watches Athens vote on the Pnyx

b: In 431 BC war broke out between Athens and Sparta, and Thucydides tells us he began writing at its very start, believing it would be the greatest war the Greeks had ever fought. On one side stood Athens, a sea power, rich, democratic and restless. On the other stood Sparta, a land power, austere, conservative and controlling a league of allies in the Peloponnese, the southern peninsula of Greece.

Thucydides lets both sides speak before the war. The Corinthians, Sparta's allies, complain that the Athenians are innovators, quick to plan and quick to act, never at rest and never letting anyone else rest, while the Spartans are slow, cautious and content with what they have. The old Spartan king Archidamus urges patience. Athens, he warns, is rich and commands the sea, and this will not be a short war. His people vote for war anyway.

The immediate causes were a string of quarrels: a dispute over Corcyra, a naval power off the west coast; a rebellion at Potidaea in the north; Athenian trade sanctions against Megara. Thucydides lists them carefully. Then he says something that has made him famous. The truest cause, he writes, though the least spoken of, was the growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta, which made war inevitable.

This is a startling move. He separates the surface reasons people give from the deeper structural force underneath them. In recent years the American political scientist Graham Allison has called this pattern the Thucydides Trap: the danger of war when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one. Some classicists think Allison stretches Thucydides too far, and that the war was less inevitable than the phrase suggests. But the core insight is plain. Fear of a shifting balance can push rivals into conflict that neither fully wants.
ch.cap: Athens' power grows and its shadow falls on Sparta

b: Pericles had a strategy. Athens could not beat Sparta's army on land, so it would not try. The people of Attica would move inside the city walls and the Long Walls running down to the port of Piraeus. The Spartans could burn the farms, but Athens would be supplied by sea, use its navy to raid the enemy coast, and simply outlast them. Avoid risks, he warned, and do not try to expand the empire while the war goes on.

At the end of the first year, Pericles gave the funeral oration for the Athenian dead, and Thucydides records it at length. It is a portrait of Athens at its proudest: a democracy where power belongs to the many, where men are judged on merit, where people love beauty without extravagance and wisdom without softness. He called the city an education to Greece.

A warning about the speeches in this book. Thucydides tells us openly that he could not remember speeches word for word, whether he heard them himself or from others. So he wrote what he thought each speaker would have needed to say, keeping as close as possible to the general sense of what was actually said. The speeches are therefore partly his own reconstruction, and they are where he puts much of his analysis.
ch.cap: Pericles praises the war dead beside the coffins

b: In the summer of 430 BC, with the whole population of Attica crammed inside the walls, a plague arrived by sea. Thucydides caught it himself and survived, and he describes it so precisely, the fever, the burning thirst, the sores, the loss of memory in survivors, so that people could recognise it if it ever returned. Scholars still argue over what it was. Typhus and typhoid fever are the most common suggestions.

He is even more interested in what it did to people's character. Doctors died first, because they were nearest the sick. Bodies lay in the temples. With death so near, people stopped fearing the gods or the law, since nobody expected to live long enough to be punished. They spent their money quickly on pleasure. Honour, which takes time to earn, seemed pointless.

In 429 BC Pericles himself died, probably of the plague. Thucydides judges that his successors were more equal to each other and each grasped for first place, and so they began to hand affairs over to the whims of the people. With the steadying hand gone, the strategy of patience began to break down.
ch.cap: Plague pyres burn at night inside crowded Athens

b: In 427 BC the city of Mytilene, on the island of Lesbos, rebelled against Athens and was crushed. In a fury the assembly voted to kill all the men and enslave the women and children, and sent a ship to carry out the order. The next day many citizens had second thoughts. A demagogue named Cleon argued for sticking to the decision, saying an empire is a tyranny and must be ruled by fear. A man named Diodotus replied that harshness would only make future rebels fight to the death. Diodotus narrowly won, and a second ship raced across the Aegean, its crew eating as they rowed, and arrived just in time.

The same year, on Corcyra, a civil war broke out between democrats and oligarchs, each side backed by one of the great powers. Thucydides' account of it is among the darkest pages in ancient literature. Fathers killed sons. Men were dragged from temples. And words themselves changed their meaning. Reckless daring was called loyal courage. Prudent hesitation was called cowardice. Moderation was a cover for weakness.

This is one of his deepest insights. In war, he says, people lose the easy circumstances of daily life, and war is a violent teacher that brings most people's characters down to the level of their circumstances. Under pressure, a society does not just make bad decisions. It changes the vocabulary it uses to judge them.
ch.cap: The reprieve ship races, rowers eating at the oars

b: In 425 BC fortune swung dramatically. An Athenian force fortified a headland at Pylos, on the Spartan coast, and trapped a body of Spartan soldiers on the little island of Sphacteria. Cleon, who had mocked the generals for their slowness, boasted that he could finish the job in twenty days. To everyone's astonishment, he did. Around a hundred and twenty Spartans of full citizen rank surrendered rather than die, which shocked the Greek world, because Spartans were supposed never to give up. Sparta sued for peace, and Athens, flushed with success, refused.

In 424 BC Thucydides was elected one of Athens' ten generals and sent to the north Aegean, where his family had connections. The Spartan general Brasidas, perhaps the most able commander on either side, marched on Amphipolis, a vital Athenian colony near the Thracian silver and timber. Thucydides was with his ships at Thasos, half a day's sail away. He arrived in time to save the nearby port of Eion, but Amphipolis had already surrendered.

Athens punished failure harshly. Thucydides tells us, in a single plain sentence, that he was exiled for twenty years after his command at Amphipolis. He does not complain or defend himself. He simply adds that the exile gave him the chance to see events from both sides, and particularly from the Peloponnesian side, and to study them at leisure.

So the general became the historian. He set out his method. He would not rely on poets who exaggerate or on chroniclers who aim to please. He checked eyewitness accounts against each other, noting that witnesses of the same event gave different reports, from faulty memory or from partiality. He expected his work might seem less entertaining for lacking romance. But he wrote it, he said, not as a prize essay for the moment but as a possession for all time.

The war in the north went on without him. In 422 BC both Cleon and Brasidas were killed in battle at Amphipolis. Thucydides observes, with grim understatement, that with the two men most opposed to peace gone, both sides were ready to talk. In 421 BC the Peace of Nicias was signed, meant to last fifty years. It was never really kept, and Thucydides insists that it was not a true peace at all but a pause within a single long war.
ch.cap: Too late for Amphipolis, Thucydides walks into exile

b: In 416 BC, during an uneasy truce, Athens sent a fleet to the small island of Melos, a Spartan colony that had stayed neutral. The Athenian envoys demanded surrender. Thucydides stages their conversation with the Melian leaders as a dialogue, and it is one of the most chilling passages in any history book.

The Athenians refuse to talk about justice. Justice, they say, only comes into question between equals in power. Otherwise the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. The Melians appeal to fairness, to hope, to the gods, to the chance that Sparta will rescue them. The Athenians dismiss every argument. Hope, they say, is an expensive comfort for people with nothing else.

The Melians refused to yield. After a siege the city fell, the men were killed and the women and children enslaved. Thucydides offers no comment at all. He simply places this episode immediately before the next great decision Athens made, and lets the reader feel the arrogance building.
ch.cap: Athens tells Melos: the strong do what they can

b: In 415 BC the assembly voted to send a huge expedition to conquer Sicily, a large island most voters, Thucydides says, knew almost nothing about. The cautious general Nicias warned against it and, hoping to put people off, said it would need an enormous force. The plan backfired. The crowd became even keener. The brilliant, vain young aristocrat Alcibiades argued for the expedition and was made one of its commanders.

Then it fell apart. Alcibiades was recalled to face charges of sacrilege, escaped, and defected to Sparta, where he advised the enemy on how to hurt Athens. The siege of Syracuse dragged on. Sparta sent a general, Gylippus. Athens sent reinforcements, doubling down. In 413 BC, after the Athenian fleet was trapped and beaten in the harbour of Syracuse, the army tried to retreat overland and was destroyed. Thousands of prisoners were worked to death in the stone quarries.

One detail shows how it went wrong. The retreat had been delayed by something Thucydides plainly thought absurd. In late August 413 BC, just as the Athenians were ready to slip away from Syracuse, there was an eclipse of the moon. Nicias, who was deeply superstitious, accepted the soothsayers' advice to wait twenty-seven days. By the time they tried to move, the Syracusans had blocked the harbour. Thucydides records the decision without mockery, but the reader feels the cost of leadership by omen.

Thucydides sums it up in grave, simple words. They were utterly and entirely defeated; their sufferings were on an enormous scale; army, fleet and everything were destroyed, and few out of many returned home. Here is the pattern he has been building all along: fear, then the corruption of language and judgement, then the crowd's overconfidence, then catastrophe.
ch.cap: An eclipse halts Nicias as Syracuse closes the harbour

b: Athens fought on for nine more years, with remarkable resilience, but in 404 BC it surrendered to Sparta, which had by then taken Persian money to build a fleet. The Long Walls were pulled down to the music of flute girls. Thucydides tells us he lived through the whole war and saw its end, and he was presumably allowed home after the surrender.

Yet his book does not reach that point. It breaks off in the winter of 411 BC, in the middle of a narrative, almost mid-sentence. We do not know why. The most likely explanation is that he died, around 400 BC, before he could finish. Later writers, including Xenophon, picked up the story where he left it.

His reputation has only grown. Thomas Hobbes translated him into English in 1629. Modern international relations scholars treat him as a founder of realism, the view that states act out of fear, honour and interest. Historians admire his method while noting that he was not neutral. He had reasons to dislike Cleon, who may have helped to have him exiled, and his speeches are partly his own invention.

Underneath everything sits a simple theory of human behaviour, which he lets Athenian envoys state early in the book. Defending their empire before the Spartans, they say that they were driven to it by three of the strongest motives: fear, honour and interest. Every state, they suggest, would behave the same in their position. Thucydides does not entirely endorse them, but almost every event in the history can be read through those three words.

But his central claim has held up remarkably. As long as human nature stays the same, he wrote, events like these will happen again in similar ways. That is why the exiled general bothered to write it all down.
ch.cap: The scroll breaks off mid-sentence as the walls fall

take: Thucydides separated the quarrels people argued about from the truest cause, fear of shifting power. In any dispute, ask what deeper fear or change is driving the stated complaint.
Pericles' patient plan collapsed once rivals competed for popularity after his death. Write your strategy down and build succession so it survives the loss of one person.
In Corcyra, recklessness was renamed courage and caution renamed cowardice. When a team starts redefining words to excuse bad behaviour, stop and reset.
Athens voted to massacre Mytilene, then changed its mind the next day just in time. Build a cooling-off period into big decisions made in anger.

The strong do what they can, said the Athenians at Melos, and Athens was later destroyed by the coalition its arrogance helped build. Treat smaller partners and customers fairly even when you could squeeze them.
Nicias's attempt to scare voters off Sicily only made them keener. When enthusiasm for a project runs ahead of knowledge, slow down and gather facts.
Athens reinforced failure in Sicily instead of cutting losses. Set clear exit points before big ventures.
Thucydides compared witnesses because memory and bias distort. Before acting on a report, get a second account.
recall: What did Thucydides call the truest cause of the war?
The growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta. He separated this deeper cause from the specific quarrels over Corcyra, Potidaea and Megara.
How did Thucydides handle the speeches in his book?
He admitted he could not remember them exactly, so he wrote what each speaker would likely have needed to say, keeping close to the general sense. They are partly his own reconstruction.
What happened to Thucydides after Amphipolis?
He arrived too late to stop Brasidas taking the city in 424 BC and was exiled for twenty years. He used the exile to gather information from both sides.
What is the core argument of the Melian dialogue?
The Athenians argued that justice only applies between equals and that the strong do what they can while the weak suffer what they must. Melos refused to yield and was destroyed.
Why did the Sicilian expedition fail?
Athens voted for it in ignorance and overconfidence, lost its best commander Alcibiades to defection, then reinforced a failing siege. In 413 BC the fleet and army were destroyed.
note: Nearly everything known of Thucydides' life comes from his own text, including his illness, his command at Amphipolis and his twenty-year exile; the family's Thracian gold mine connection rests on that text and later ancient biographers. The speeches are acknowledged reconstructions. The identity of the plague is debated. Graham Allison's Thucydides Trap is a modern framing that several classicists consider an oversimplification, and Thucydides' judgements of figures such as Cleon may reflect personal bias.
words: Leadership or dominance of one state or group over others.
Athens turned a voluntary alliance against Persia into a hegemony that collected tribute, and Sparta's fear of that growing power was, for Thucydides, the truest cause of the war.
A politician who wins support by stirring popular passions rather than by reasoned argument.
Thucydides casts Cleon as the demagogue who urged Athens to massacre the men of Mytilene, though Cleon may have helped get him exiled, so the portrait may not be neutral.
Thucydides places the brutal Melian dialogue just before the Sicilian expedition, letting the reader watch Athenian hubris build towards catastrophe.
The quality of seeming true or real.
Thucydides admits his speeches are reconstructions of what each speaker would have needed to say, so they aim at verisimilitude rather than word for word accuracy.
The practice of reading signs and omens to decide what to do.
Nicias trusted augury when the moon was eclipsed at Syracuse in 413 BC, delayed the retreat twenty-seven days, and lost the army.
stories: The race of the second ship

In 427 BC the city of Mytilene rebelled against Athens and was crushed. In a fury the Athenian assembly voted to kill every man and enslave the women and children, and a ship sailed to carry out the order. Overnight, many citizens had second thoughts. The next day Cleon argued that an empire must rule by fear; Diodotus answered that harshness only makes future rebels fight to the death. Diodotus narrowly won. A second ship set off a day behind, its crew eating as they rowed. It arrived just as the first order was being read out. A whole city was saved by a change of heart and hard rowing.
The eclipse that cost an army

By late August 413 BC the Athenian siege of Syracuse had failed and the army was finally ready to slip away by sea. Then the moon went into eclipse. The commander, Nicias, was deeply superstitious, and he accepted the soothsayers' advice to wait twenty-seven days before moving. By the time the Athenians tried to leave, the Syracusans had blocked the harbour. The fleet was beaten, the army was destroyed on the overland retreat, and thousands of prisoners were worked to death in the stone quarries. Thucydides records the decision without mockery, but the lesson needs no comment: an omen made the decision that judgement should have made.
The general who lost a city and found a book

In 424 BC Thucydides was one of Athens' ten elected generals, posted to the north Aegean with a fleet at Thasos. The brilliant Spartan Brasidas marched on Amphipolis, a vital Athenian colony. Thucydides sailed for half a day and arrived in time to save the nearby port of Eion, but Amphipolis had already surrendered. Athens punished failure hard, and he tells us in a single plain sentence that he was exiled for twenty years. He neither complains nor defends himself. He simply notes that exile let him see the war from both sides. The failed general became the historian who wrote, he said, a possession for all time.
biz: On Corcyra, Thucydides saw words change meaning: recklessness became courage and caution became cowardice. Sales teams under target pressure drift the same way, so pestering becomes persistence and a hesitant debt client becomes someone to push over the line. This week, write down your contact rules in plain words: maximum call and WhatsApp attempts per lead, a clear opt-out honoured immediately, and what staff must do when a client shows signs of vulnerability. Review a sample of recorded calls monthly against those words, not against how the team describes them. Track complaints, opt-outs and vulnerability flags as closely as conversions.
Write your Sicily memo before any big venture

Athens voted for Sicily knowing almost nothing about the island, then doubled down with reinforcements when it went wrong. Before any major new move, such as a new ad channel, a new brand or the appointed representative route to advising directly, write one page on what you actually know: the regulatory permissions required, realistic volumes, cost and capacity. Then set your exit rule in advance, for example: if cost per completed case on a new channel is above a set figure after six weeks, stop rather than send another fleet. Decide the rule while calm, and keep it when the moon goes dark.
connects: Machiavelli and Thucydides are the two founding realists, both describing power as it is practised rather than as moralists wish it were, and the Melian dialogue reads like a chapter of The Prince.
The Athenian assembly's swing from massacre to mercy overnight, and its overconfident vote for Sicily, are textbook cases of the fast, emotional judgement Kahneman calls System 1.
Tuchman shows the great powers of 1914, like Athens and Sparta, sliding into war through fear of a shifting balance that no one could talk their way out of.
recap:
Around four hundred and sixty years before Christ, a rich boy was born in Athens. His name was Thucydides, his family owned gold mining rights in Thrace, and he grew up in the city's golden age, under the great speaker Pericles, as the Parthenon rose above him. He watched thousands of citizens vote on war and peace, and that democracy under strain became the subject of his life.

In the year war broke out between Athens and Sparta, he began to write, convinced it would be the greatest war the Greeks had ever fought. His first big idea is about causes. People gave many reasons for the war, but the truest cause, he wrote, was the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta. Underneath the quarrels sat a shifting balance, and fear.

The second idea is about how fragile a society's morals are. A plague struck Athens, crammed inside its walls. Thucydides caught it and survived. He watched people stop fearing the gods or the law, because no one expected to live long enough to be punished. Pericles died, and steadier strategy died with him.

The third idea is that under pressure even words change their meaning. In a civil war on Corcyra, reckless daring was called loyal courage and caution was called cowardice. War, he said, is a violent teacher.

Then his own turn came. Elected a general, he arrived too late to save the city of Amphipolis, and Athens exiled him for twenty years. He used the exile to see the war from both sides and to write carefully, checking witness against witness.

His fourth idea is the arrogance of power. At Melos, the Athenians told a small neutral island that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Thucydides offers no comment. He simply places it next to Athens' next decision: a vast expedition to Sicily, voted for by people who knew almost nothing about the island. It ended in total destruction, hastened by a general who delayed the retreat because of an eclipse of the moon.

His fifth idea ties it together. States act from fear, honour and interest, and as long as human nature stays the same, events like these will happen again. His history breaks off almost mid sentence, and he probably died before finishing it.

The line to remember: watch the fear beneath the reasons, because that is what really moves people.
